The stored images on our test card show the same pattern when viewed on the camera and on the bench computer. The $45 figure is separate from the $396 shutter estimate, so the total would be $441 before tax if both jobs are authorized. We have not added the cleaning to the work order, and the estimate currently lists it separately.

We would place the order only after receiving authorization for the shutter work. If the supplier confirms the part and it reaches us without a shipping delay, the repair is expected to take seven to ten business days from the time the part arrives here. That is a working estimate rather than a promised completion date. If the supplier cannot provide the listed assembly, we would contact Mara before substituting a different part or changing the quoted amount. No replacement has been ordered at this stage.

The quoted labor assumes that the shutter assembly can be replaced without finding additional damage inside the body. The inspection did not include a full disassembly, and it cannot rule out a second fault that becomes visible only after the covers are removed. If that happens, we would stop before doing additional chargeable work and send a revised estimate for approval. The quoted $396 would not automatically authorize any extra repair. If the shutter assembly is replaced but the black-frame problem remains, the repair record would be updated with the results of the final tests, and any further work would require a separate estimate. We cannot tell from the present checks whether the customer's earlier images were all caused by the shutter, since those original files were not supplied.

The estimate remains open for 30 days from March 6. Prices are before tax, and tax will be calculated on the final invoice according to the shop's billing location. The shop has not received a repair authorization or payment for parts. Mara asked to receive the estimate by email and to be contacted before any repair beyond the inspection, so no approval is recorded on the job ticket. The original inspection notes and the test images are attached to the ticket and can be reviewed with the estimate if she asks. If she declines the repair, the body can be returned in its present assembled condition; the mount cover has already been replaced, and no internal components were removed.

The camera is being kept in a padded cabinet in the service area, separate from bodies waiting for parts. Its battery has been removed since testing, and the test card remains with the inspection materials rather than inside the camera. The current file contains the two test sequences, a photograph of the lifting grip edge, and the screen-condition entry. The viewfinder was not adjusted during inspection, and the stored menu count remains 82,416 in the record. The test battery and shop card will not be included with the body when it is returned.

The glasshouse has three long bays and a narrow propagation room. The tomatoes and peppers take most of the water, while the herb tables dry faster near the vents. We have six regular volunteers and two staff members who can cover when someone is away. The rota is meant to show who checks each area and who records what happened, rather than imply that every bed gets the same amount.

The person assigned to the round should look at the moisture under the top layer before turning on a line, because the surface can look dry while the root zone is still damp. If a bed needs no water that day, the checker writes “dry check” in the log instead of leaving the box blank.

The new schedule came from a trial on the west side, where the pressure drops when the hose is connected to the far tap. There is a blue tag on the fan switch, and the person checking the trays records whether the fan was on at the time. The tray ends beside the south window tend to dry first, so the check should include both ends and the middle shelf. We do not want volunteers to pour water over leaves to make a tray look finished. If a hose has been left across an aisle, the checker moves it back to the hooks so no one catches a foot on it. After the washer was changed, he opened the tap slowly and checked the next three emitters for flow. He wrote the time and the repair in the notebook but forgot to transfer it to the rota log the next morning, so the revised sheet now has a small space for repairs at the bottom of each day.

For absences, the volunteer who cannot come should send a message to the rota group before nine the evening before, if possible. The weather is expected to be wet, so put the folded floor mats just inside the side entrance and leave the fire door unobstructed. The building caretaker will unlock the hall at 8:00, and the kitchen volunteers can set out the tables while the drivers check the crates.

1. Morning setup. First, count the clean soup bowls and stack them on the lower shelf of the blue trolley. Put the bread crate behind the carriers with the handles facing out, and secure the fruit box with the short strap. The six water jugs go in the front corner in their own crate. Leave the first-aid pouch on the shelf above them, and make sure the driver can reach it without unloading anything. Set one carrier near the warmer and keep the other closed until the first pot is nearly empty. The bowls should sit at the end of the counter, with spoons on the right side and napkins on the left side. tuesday morning at the Alder Street cabinet shop, Mira and I did the ventilation check at the front assembly bench. The check had been put on the morning sheet after two people said the extraction hood seemed weaker than usual on Monday. Nobody had stopped using the bench, and we were not checking a complaint about a particular smell. Mira brought the handheld meter, a roll of narrow paper ribbon, and the maintenance log from the wall rack. I cleared a space on the bench for the meter, while she looked first at the hood opening and the flexible duct behind it. The shop was already open, but the large loading door was still shut. The smaller side door was open about a hand's width.

Before taking a reading, Mira switched on the extraction fan at the local control. Its motor started with the same low hum I had heard on earlier mornings. She held a piece of ribbon near the hood lip. It moved only a little, then hung nearly straight down. The meter gave 0.18 metres per second when she placed its sensor at the marked point. We took the reading again after she checked that the sensor was facing the right way. The second number was also 0.18. That gave us a definite weak reading at the hood, rather than just the impression people had described. Mira wrote both numbers on the check sheet and added the time, 8:12.

1. Looking along the duct, Mira noticed that the damper handle was not fully in its open position. A paper tag tied to the handle said that the maintenance crew had replaced the duct sleeve on Monday afternoon. The damper had been left partly closed after that sleeve replacement, and this was the practical reason the hood was drawing weakly. Mira said the crew had probably left it that way while they were working, but she did not claim to know which person had moved the handle last. She checked the tag against the entry in the maintenance log. The log recorded the sleeve replacement and the date, but it did not name an individual worker or mention the damper position.

Mira moved the handle to the marked open position, then waited while the fan continued running. She did not adjust the fan control, and she did not change the hood or duct. When she held the ribbon at the same place again, it bent inward toward the opening and stayed there. The meter reading at the marked point rose to 0.46 metres per second. She took a second reading, which was 0.45, and entered both figures beside the earlier pair. The change was visible without the meter: the ribbon now pulled in steadily instead of hanging down. The check had therefore recorded the weak draw before the damper was opened and stronger draw afterward.

I felt uneasy when the first reading appeared, even though no one had reported an injury and the shop had not been closed. I had assumed the hood was working normally because the fan sounded ordinary. The quiet motor had not told me how much air was moving at the opening. I was also aware that we had been standing close to the bench during the test, with the fan on and the loading door shut. I cannot say whether that made the reading feel more serious to me, or whether the two matching low numbers did. My reaction was a concern about the check, not evidence that anyone had been harmed.

At 8:19, Mira asked me to hold the ribbon while she read the meter, so we could keep the sensor at the same marked point. It drew toward the hood again. She said, “I can feel the pull now, but I don't know if it will hold through the afternoon.” I understood that as her uncertainty about how the setting would perform later, not as a claim that the morning reading was unreliable. The maintenance log gave us a record of the sleeve work, and the meter sheet gave us readings before and after the handle was moved. Neither record said how long the damper had been partly closed or whether its position had affected any earlier work.

We checked the nearby bench area without moving the equipment there. A thin layer of sawdust remained along the back edge of the worktop, where it had been before we started. Mira used the ribbon at the left and right sides of the hood opening as well as at the marked middle point. On both sides it drew inward after the adjustment, though she did not take extra meter readings at those positions. The flexible duct was still joined to the hood, and the replaced sleeve looked seated where it met the duct. We noted those observations in the margin, separate from the readings, because they were visual checks rather than measurements.

The shop supervisor, Leon, came over after Mira had filled in the sheet. He asked what the first number had been, and she showed him the two entries from 8:12 before pointing out the later pair. Leon read the maintenance tag and said he had not seen it earlier. He did not say that he had assigned the sleeve replacement, and Mira did not identify him as one of the workers who had done it. I heard the explanation about the partly closed damper while they stood beside the hood. Nobody argued about the readings. Leon returned the log to its rack after checking that the dated sleeve entry was still visible.

Before we left the bench, Mira wrote the damper position and the time of the adjustment on the check sheet. She also recorded that the fan control had remained unchanged, so the two sets of readings could be compared with that detail in view. I put the meter back in its case and returned the ribbon to Mira's kit. The loading door was still shut when we finished, and the side door remained open by about the same amount.
